paragraphs: After reading today’s passage, please read the devotional below.

The Book of Romans is all about “the gospel”. The gospel of Jesus Christ is good news to the believer and an offence to the unbeliever. It calls us out of a sinful lifestyle which is uncomfortable. It unearths unhealthy human habits, addresses immoral actions and unethical decisions.

In verse 21, the Apostle Paul described the spiritual condition of Rome for us: “For although they knew God, they neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks to him.” This hypocrisy, duplicity or lukewarmness is repulsive to God. In order to become the people God wants us to be, we need to allow the gospel of Jesus Christ to transform us from the inside out.

In verse 1, the Apostle Paul described himself as “set apart for the gospel”. To be set apart means to be in the world, but not of the world. It is to do the will of God, not the will of the world and of self. In writing to Titus about God’s grace, Paul said, “It teaches us to say ‘No’ to ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives in this present age.” (Titus 2:12) In order to be set apart, we need to say YES to Jesus and NO to the devil. Are you set apart for the gospel?

In verse 15, the Apostle Paul shared that he was “eager to preach the gospel”. To preach the gospel means to tell the world of God’s grace made available through Jesus Christ. It is to evangelize all people with the hope of acceptance, even in the face of opposition. In writing to the Corinthian church, Paul said, “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!” (1 Cor. 9:16) Are you eager to preach the gospel?

In verse 16, the Apostle Paul made a confession that I hope we all will make, “I am not ashamed of the gospel.” If we have been saved by this gospel, we must hold on firmly to it and never turn our back on it. While imprisoned, Paul wrote to Timothy, “But I am not ashamed… for I know the one in whom I trust, and I am sure that he is able to guard what I have entrusted to him until the day of his return.” (2 Tim. 1:12) We are to endure because any temporary discomfort for the gospel can never outweigh the eternal reward of the gospel. Are you unashamed of the gospel?
The gospel-centered life changes everything! We become servants of the Living God, stewards of His gospel and those who are willing to surrender everything for the sake of the advancement of gospel.
Chris Padiath

paragraphs: After reading today’s passage, please read the devotional below.

Have you ever tried to justify your sin? Maybe you told yourself, I was tired or stressed; I’m only human; everyone else is doing it; or I can’t help it—it’s just the way God made me. We are often quick to make excuses to alleviate our guilt.

In this passage, Paul addresses those who were attempting to rationalize their sinful behaviour by claiming that their actions provided an opportunity for God to demonstrate his goodness and truthfulness and to bring Him glory. This is a distorted view of God’s grace. It is using His grace as freedom to sin rather than as a motivation to live rightly.

Paul refutes this reasoning and makes it clear that sin does not bring glory to God. Using God’s grace as a license to sin is not only absurd, but it’s a denial of God’s holiness. Our sin does not elevate God, but only distances us from Him and damages the testimony of His righteousness.

We may not be using the same excuses Paul addressed, but we can still be tempted torationalize sin in our lives. It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking that God’s grace covers our sin and that we can get away with it because we know He will forgive us, but this way of thinking minimizes the seriousness of sin and underestimates God’s holiness.

We may not be using the same excuses Paul addressed, but we can still be tempted to rationalize sin in our lives. It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking that God’s grace covers our sin and that we can get away with it because we know He will forgive us, but this way of thinking minimizes the seriousness of sin and underestimates God’s holiness.
Mary Ann Charters

paragraphs: After reading today’s passage, please read the devotional below.

Romans 5:1-11 highlights the profound transformation that occurs when we place our faith in Jesus Christ. Through His sacrifice, we are justified, declared right before God and given access to His grace and peace.

Through Jesus, we have peace with God, which means we are no longer separated from Him by our sin. Before Christ, we were enemies of God, but His death reconciled us, offering a deep and lasting peace. This peace is not just an absence of conflict; it’s the assurance that we are no longer under judgment, but are fully accepted by our Heavenly Father.

Paul challenges us to "boast in our sufferings", not because of the pain itself, but because suffering produces perseverance, which leads to character and ultimately hope. This hope, rooted in God’s love, does not disappoint. Instead of running from challenges, we can see them as opportunities for growth, knowing that God is shaping us to be more like His Son.

Verses six to eight demonstrate the astonishing love of God. While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. He didn’t wait for us to clean up our act. In His grace, He gave His life for those who were undeserving. This is the ultimate display of love—sacrificial, unconditional and complete. It is a love that reaches us in our brokenness and offers us forgiveness.

Through Christ, we have been reconciled to God. This reconciliation is not just a past event, but a present reality. We are now in right relationship with God and this brings a joy that no one and nothing can take away. We can "boast in God" because of what Jesus has done for us—His life, death, and resurrection—secure our standing before the Father.
So how does this apply to us today?
We need to reflect on the peace we have with God through Jesus. We can rest in this truth, allowing it to calm our hearts, no matter the circumstance. He has our back!

When trials come (and they surely will), remember that God can use them to shape our character and deepen our hope in him. You can be assured that God has not forgotten about you. You are precious to Him.
Remember Christ died for us while we were still sinners. He loved us before we ever loved him. Let His love fill you with gratitude.
Celebrate the fact that you are now in a right relationship with God because of Jesus’ sacrifice.
Stephen Gawne

paragraphs: After reading today’s passage, please read the devotional below.

There is a popular movie with a catchy title that you may have heard of called “Mission Impossible”. It features Tom Cruise, an agent who seems to defy the odds in solving complex problems and bringing closure to complicated situations.

Many today view the life of faith as “mission impossible.” Desiring to do good or what is right, many people turn to religion to help them become better. They may be familiar with the Old Testament law, and perhaps, even tried to obey its rules unsuccessfully. In giving up, they feel that it is a standard that is unattainable.

For Israel, the Mosaic Law was a reminder of the commands God had instructed them to obey. It revealed a holiness code that was quite different from the nations around them. But even for Israel, who was bound by the Law, upholding the Law was mission impossible with them struggling to keep its commands. In their despair, God provided them with a promise that one day there would be another way. (cf. Jer. 31:33)

In Romans 7, Paul highlights the important issues of sin and death, along with Law and the life in the Spirit. In his metaphor, Paul likens the Law as a marriage commitment with us being legally bound to it until death. With us being bound to the Law, we are under its obligations, but Christ’s death and resurrection changes things. Through His work, we are freed from the Law of sin and death. As Christians, we are no longer bound by these things, and instead, we are now raised to life with Christ and can live free from the bondage of sin and produce godly fruit. What is impossible for us to do on our own has become possible through Christ’s work on our behalf.

So what does this practically mean for us? Well, take a moment to reflect on your life. Is there something you are struggling to overcome? Is there some sort of sin or behaviour that you just can’t seem to break? Remember, what is mission impossible for us is now possible through Christ's death and resurrection. He can help us overcome those areas of struggle and help us break from the chains of sin. By faith, embrace the victory of Christ’s resurrection and receive your victory that raises you from a life burdened by sin.
Christalyn Weigert

paragraphs: After reading today’s passage, please read the devotional below.

Have you ever found yourself comparing the circumstances of your life to that of others?  After scrolling social media, have you found yourself feeling unsatisfied with your life because you have just been met with an endless highlight reel of others living the “good life”? If so, you may be inclined to think the Bible would prohibit this type of self-examination, since it may lead to covetousness and discontentment, but you would be wrong. The Bible encourages us to start comparing our circumstances to an ideal, but not the ideal of what “could have been”; no that is a losing battle. We need to start comparing our circumstances against what "will be".

This is precisely what Paul encourages us to do in the reading for today. In verses 18-19, he tackles the question of how a Christian is to respond to suffering. Paul knew a thing or two about suffering; he faced beatings, imprisonment, shipwrecks, and even stoning for the sake of the gospel. Paul is speaking from first-hand experience when he says, “I consider that our present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed in us.” In other words, when we compare our current struggles in light of the future glory promised to us, there’s really no comparison. I love how Paul puts it in 2 Corinthians 4:17 where he describes it this way, “for this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison.” Paul is teaching us that when compared to our future glory, our present afflictions are light and momentary.

It might seem that Paul is downplaying our current sufferings and encouraging a form of stoicism in the face of it, but is that really what is going on here? No, I don’t think so.  Look at verse 28, a verse that will be familiar to many, “And we know that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according to his purpose.” There is a clear purpose in our afflictions, and that purpose is ultimately for our good, not just some of our afflictions, but all of them. God is actively using the situations of our lives to mold us into the kind of children He desires; children that will one day be heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. This eternal perspective can make all the difference in your life.
C.S. Lewis gives us a unique perspective on what Paul is getting at:

It would seem that Our Lord finds our desires not too strong, but too weak. We are half-hearted creatures, fooling about with drink and sex and ambition when infinite joy is offered us, like an ignorant child who wants to go on making mud pies in a slum because he cannot imagine what is meant by the offer of a holiday at the sea. We are far too easily pleased. (The Weight of Glory, and Other Addresses)

The next time you find yourself comparing your circumstances with someone else’s and you find yourself coming up short, take a moment to reflect on the glories promised to you in Christ. You will find that the things of earth will grow strangely dim in the light of His glory and grace.
Andrew Lucas

paragraphs: After reading today’s passage, please read the devotional below.

Starting with Abraham, the Hebrews, also known as Jews, were the people of God. The nation of Israel had been set apart from all the other nations of the world. While the salvation story of God started with the Jews, it does not end there.

In Romans 10:1-13, the Apostle Paul shared his heartfelt longing for his own people, Israel, to experience salvation. Although his mission was to the Gentiles, he showed concern for the Jews. The Jews believed that following the Law was the only way to attain righteousness with God, but keeping the Law was very hard and always impossible to uphold perfectly. To break one law was to break the entire law.

Paul then explained that true salvation is obtained by faith alone in Jesus Christ. He explained that salvation through Christ is already present and not an unachievable task. In Romans 10:5-8, he reviewed that Christ had already come down from heaven, died for our sins and defeated death so that by believing with our heart and confessing with our mouth, it is possible for us to attain salvation.

Do you remember the day of your salvation? Do you remember your belief in Christ and your confession of faith? Simply having faith in Jesus means “believing” in His death and resurrection and “confessing” His Lordship over your life is what leads to our salvation. Paul goes on to say that this salvation is available to all and that anyone who calls on the name of the Lord Jesus Christ will not be put to shame, but will be saved. This is God’s promise to everyone, no matter who they are or where they come from. His love and salvation are freely given to all who put their trust in Him. The beauty of this truth is that we don’t have to climb mountains or cross seas to find salvation. Salvation is a divine conviction that is known in our hearts and is declared with our mouths (Rom. 10:9-10). God has made his grace accessible; we just need to believe and accept. It’s an open invitation, reminding us that salvation is about His grace, not our performance.

Romans 10:1-13 also reminds us that God’s love and salvation are deeply personal, always near and available to anyone who reaches out in faith. Is there anyone in your life who needs to be saved? May I encourage you to share this gospel and intercede for their salvation. As we pray for the salvation of all those who are far from Christ, let us also remember to pray for the peace of Israel and the diaspora of Jews all over the world. May they recognize Jesus as their long-awaited Messiah.
Siju Mathew

paragraphs: After reading today’s passage, please read the devotional below.

As someone who has experienced God’s mercies, do you want to honour God with your life and wonder what a wholly yielded life to God looks like? In Romans 12:1-2, Paul outlines three essential demands of a life wholly devoted to God. He appeals to us to offer our bodies as a living sacrifice, resist conformity to the world's patterns and be transformed by renewing our minds.

To follow Jesus requires full commitment to Christ's cause. Paul first urges us to offer our bodies as a living sacrifice. This is a call to total surrender to God. In the Old Testament, priests sacrificed animals on the altar, yielding every right, interest and authority over that sacrifice to God. The dead animal on the altar is wholly given to God. Here, Paul calls us to yield our entire being, including our bodies, to the Lord as a living sacrifice. God wants all of us, not just a part of us. Today, will you offer the Lord your body, interests and entire being?

Next, Paul urges us to resist conforming to the world's patterns. The dominant culture often rebels against God, enabling our selfish and sinful nature to live in ways that are not consistent with God's will. We cannot live like chameleons. A chameleon almost always adopts the color of its environment. As followers of Christ, we cannot adopt the world's ways. We are not conformists. Though we live in this world, we are called to be different (John 17:16). How will you live out this truth today?

Finally, Paul encourages us to be transformed by renewing our minds. The Christian life is a process, not an event. The word “transformed” suggests a process of change. While salvation may be instantaneous, character, values and behavior transform over time as we obey God's Word. This transformation makes a difference in our lives, marriages and communities. Being changed into the image of Christ through the process of transformation should be the desire of every follower of Christ. One of the ways this transformation happens in the Christian community is through discipleship, as we study and obey God's Word together with other believers. What commitment will you make today to engage in personal transformation?

paragraphs: After reading today’s passage, please read the devotional below.

In this passage, Paul is highlighting the friction that existed in early church life. While the specifics might differ in our context, the heart of Paul’s message is what we need to heed. As Christians, we need to determine what is moral, ethical and legal when it comes to conduct in private and public. While at a personal level, we might think our comfort level or preferences should be respected or adopted by others, we need to think about how our freedom and rights might negatively impact the body of Christ. We must accept Christians who are weaker or less mature than ourselves into fellowship without passing judgement on them because of their convictions. (cf. Rom. 14:1)

While we need to agree on our biblical convictions, there are some things that may feel permissible, but may not be beneficial for all (cf. 1 Cor. 10:23). The temptation is to compare ourselves with others. We often end up thinking that our faith is better or that others are inferior. These conclusions bring about division and disunity in the body of Christ. In Romans 14:13, we read, “Therefore let us stop passing judgment on one another. Instead, make up your mind not to put any stumbling block or obstacle in the way of a brother or sister.” Then later in verse 21, we read, “It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything else that will cause your brother or sister to fall.”  Paul is pointing out how we can hurt someone through our Christian liberties and by not respecting differing convictions.

Romans 14:18 tells that we need to uphold our convictions before God, but allow others to give an account to God for themselves. In the pursuit of unity, let us not impose on others, but rather, be supportive and encouraging to other Christians to focus on Christ and His standard of righteousness. Paul ends by leaving us with a worthy goal for all of us to aspire toward: “So then, let us pursue the things that make for peace and the building up of one another.” (Rom.14:19)
Dan Nesseth

verses.1: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea.
verses.2: I ask you to receive her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints and to give her any help she may need from you, for she has been a great help to many people, including me.
verses.3: Greet Priscilla and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus.
verses.4: They risked their lives for me. Not only I but all the churches of the Gentiles are grateful to them.
verses.5: Greet also the church that meets at their house. Greet my dear friend Epenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.
verses.6: Greet Mary, who worked very hard for you.
verses.7: Greet Andronicus and Junias, my relatives who have been in prison with me. They are outstanding among the apostles, and they were in Christ before I was.
verses.8: Greet Ampliatus, whom I love in the Lord.
verses.9: Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my dear friend Stachys.
verses.10: Greet Apelles, tested and approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus.
verses.11: Greet Herodion, my relative. Greet those in the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.
verses.12: Greet Tryphena and Tryphosa, those women who work hard in the Lord. Greet my dear friend Persis, another woman who has worked very hard in the Lord.
verses.13: Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me, too.
verses.14: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas and the brothers with them.
verses.15: Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas and all the saints with them.
verses.16: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ send greetings.
verses.17: I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and put obstacles in your way that are contrary to the teaching you have learned. Keep away from them.
verses.18: For such people are not serving our Lord Christ, but their own appetites. By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the minds of naive people.
verses.19: Everyone has heard about your obedience, so I am full of joy over you; but I want you to be wise about what is good, and innocent about what is evil.
verses.20: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus be with you.
verses.21: Timothy, my fellow worker, sends his greetings to you, as do Lucius, Jason and Sosipater, my relatives.
verses.22: I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verses.23: Gaius, whose hospitality I and the whole church here enjoy, sends you his greetings. Erastus, who is the city's director of public works, and our brother Quartus send you their greetings.
verses.24: See Footnote
verses.25: Now to him who is able to establish you by my gospel and the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery hidden for long ages past,
verses.26: but now revealed and made known through the prophetic writings by the command of the eternal God, so that all nations might believe and obey him--
verses.27: to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen.
